Bellman Updates from Samples

The two previous chapters assumed that the Bellman operator could be evaluated exactly at any state. Every target (Lvk)(si)(\Bellman v_k)(s_i)(Lvk​)(si​) contains an expectation over the successor state,

(Lv)(s)=max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a)},(\Bellman v)(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a)\right\},(Lv)(s)=a∈As​max​{r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a)},
(1)

and the fishery computed it with a 21-node quadrature rule, while the eight-dimensional stopping problem already replaced it by an average over 32 random draws. This chapter asks what that replacement costs, and what it makes possible. When the transition density is unavailable, because the model is a simulator or a log of recorded transitions, sampling is the only way to evaluate the operator, and the sample average is the estimator. Its error is random rather than systematic, its rate does not depend on the dimension of the state, and it adds to the per-iteration error that the previous chapter bounded. Replacing exact expectations by samples is what turns the approximate dynamic programming of the previous chapters into what the operations research community calls simulation-based dynamic programming and the machine learning community calls reinforcement learning.

Two consequences of sampling organize the chapter. Acting on a value function vvv requires the expectation for every action at every decision, so with samples it requires simulation at decision time; storing the value of each action instead, the action-value function q(s,a)q(s,a)q(s,a), moves that work into training. And the maximum over noisy estimates is biased upward, even though each estimate is unbiased, so the targets of every sampled Bellman update overestimate, and the chapter ends with the ways to correct it.

Learning Goals

After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Locate the two expectations in a fitted Bellman update, inside the operator and over the states, and bound the effect of estimating either one on the fixed point

  • Replace an expectation by a sample average, state the bias and variance of the result, and explain why its rate is independent of the dimension

  • Define the action-value function and its Bellman operator, and explain what it saves at decision time

  • Derive the upward bias of a maximum over noisy estimates, and explain how decoupling selection from evaluation removes part of it

Prerequisites: fitted value iteration and its error bound (previous chapter), basic probability (expectation, variance, the central limit theorem, Jensen’s inequality).

Two Expectations in Every Fitted Update¶

Integrals appear in two places in a fitted Bellman update. The first is inside the operator: the transition expectation ∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a)\int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a)∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a) that every target contains. The second is over the states: Galerkin and least-squares conditions integrate the residual against test functions, and a regression averages the fitting error over the states where targets were computed. Collocation has only the first integral, which is one reason it was the simplest case.

Write L~\BellmanQuadL for the Bellman operator with the transition expectation replaced by a numerical rule, deterministic or random, and let fitted value iteration run with it, vk+1=P L~vkv_{k+1} = \Proj\,\BellmanQuad v_kvk+1​=PLvk​. The error after one iteration splits into three pieces by the triangle inequality. With v⋆=Lv⋆v^\star = \Bellman v^\starv⋆=Lv⋆,

∥v⋆−vk+1∥=∥v⋆−PL~vk∥≤∥v⋆−PLv⋆∥⏟best approximation+∥PLv⋆−PLvk∥⏟contraction of the current error+∥PLvk−PL~vk∥⏟integration error.\begin{aligned} \|v^\star - v_{k+1}\| &= \|v^\star - \Proj \BellmanQuad v_k\| \\ &\le \underbrace{\|v^\star - \Proj \Bellman v^\star\|}_{\text{best approximation}} + \underbrace{\|\Proj \Bellman v^\star - \Proj \Bellman v_k\|}_{\text{contraction of the current error}} + \underbrace{\|\Proj \Bellman v_k - \Proj \BellmanQuad v_k\|}_{\text{integration error}} . \end{aligned}∥v⋆−vk+1​∥​=∥v⋆−PLvk​∥≤best approximation∥v⋆−PLv⋆∥​​+contraction of the current error∥PLv⋆−PLvk​∥​​+integration error∥PLvk​−PLvk​∥​​.​
(2)

The first term is the best the basis can do, the second shrinks with the iterations when PL\Proj\BellmanPL is a contraction, and the third is the error of the integration rule, which does not shrink as the iterations proceed. In the language of Theorem 1, the integration error is one more contribution to the per-iteration error ε\varepsilonε, and it is amplified by the same 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma)1/(1−γ). This is why the accuracy of the integration rule should match the accuracy of the basis. A degree-10 Chebyshev basis represents a smooth value function to about 10-8, but with a rectangle rule for the expectation the integration error, of order h2h^2h2, dominates the sum, and the basis is wasted.

For low-dimensional problems with a smooth, explicit transition density, deterministic quadrature is the right tool, and the rule is chosen to match the basis: Gauss–Chebyshev nodes with Chebyshev polynomials, Gauss–Legendre with Legendre, Gauss–Hermite with Hermite polynomials and Gaussian shocks, midpoint or trapezoidal rules with piecewise-constant or piecewise-linear elements. With orthogonal collocation the nodes of the basis double as the nodes of the quadrature, and the expectations of the basis functions at the successors of each node can be precomputed once into a matrix, so that each iteration costs a matrix product and a maximization. The fishery used Gauss–Hermite quadrature over its log-normal shock in this way. The same pairing principle governed continuous-time trajectory optimization, where the cost integral and the dynamics were discretized on the same nodes.

Deterministic quadrature needs three things: a state of low dimension, a density that can be evaluated at the nodes, and a cheap model. The problems this part of the book is heading for have none of them. The state of the eight-dimensional stopping problem needs N8N^8N8 quadrature nodes for a product rule with NNN nodes per axis. A simulator provides draws of s′s's′ and no density. And a logged transition provides exactly one draw, which cannot be chosen. Monte Carlo integration handles all three.

Monte Carlo Integration¶

Monte Carlo integration approximates an expectation by the average of independent draws. For J=E[f(X)]J = \mathbb{E}[f(X)]J=E[f(X)] with X∼pX \sim pX∼p, draw X(1),…,X(N)∼pX^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(N)} \sim pX(1),…,X(N)∼p and form

J^N=1N∑n=1Nf(X(n)).\hat{J}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N f\big(X^{(n)}\big).J^N​=N1​n=1∑N​f(X(n)).
(3)

Two properties of this estimator carry the whole chapter. It is unbiased, E[J^N]=J\mathbb{E}[\hat{J}_N] = JE[J^N​]=J, by linearity of expectation. And its variance is σ2/N\sigma^2/Nσ2/N with σ2=Var[f(X)]\sigma^2 = \mathrm{Var}[f(X)]σ2=Var[f(X)], by independence of the draws, so by the central limit theorem

N (J^N−J)⟹N(0,σ2),\sqrt{N}\,(\hat{J}_N - J) \Longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),N​(J^N​−J)⟹N(0,σ2),
(4)

and the error decays as N−1/2N^{-1/2}N−1/2. The rate is slow next to high-order quadrature in one dimension, and it is the same in every dimension: Monte Carlo pays in variance, never in an exponential number of nodes. It is also a quadrature rule, with random nodes and equal weights 1/N1/N1/N. Importance sampling changes the distribution of the nodes and compensates with unequal weights, and the view of Monte Carlo as randomized quadrature covers it too.

The cell below checks both properties on a Gaussian with mean 2 and standard deviation 3, with 4,000 repetitions for each sample size. Before looking at the figure, predict what multiplying NNN by four does to the root mean squared error.

The Sampled Bellman Operator¶

For a fixed value function vvv and a state-action pair (s,a)(s,a)(s,a), the transition part of the Bellman operator is the expectation E[v(S′)∣S=s,A=a]\mathbb{E}[v(S') \mid S = s, A = a]E[v(S′)∣S=s,A=a]. If next states S′(1),…,S′(N)S'^{(1)}, \ldots, S'^{(N)}S′(1),…,S′(N) can be drawn from p(⋅∣s,a)p(\cdot \mid s,a)p(⋅∣s,a), by calling a simulator or by acting in the real system, the sample average estimates it. When the reward is random as well, the draws are pairs (r(n),S′(n))(r^{(n)}, S'^{(n)})(r(n),S′(n)), and the one-step return is estimated by

G^N(s,a)=1N∑n=1N[r(n)+γ v(S′(n))],\widehat{G}_N(s,a) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \Big[r^{(n)} + \gamma\, v\big(S'^{(n)}\big)\Big],GN​(s,a)=N1​n=1∑N​[r(n)+γv(S′(n))],
(5)

which is unbiased for E[r+γv(S′)∣s,a]\mathbb{E}[r + \gamma v(S') \mid s, a]E[r+γv(S′)∣s,a] as long as vvv is fixed. Substituting it into the operator gives the Monte Carlo Bellman operator

(L^Nv)(s)=max⁡a∈AsG^N(s,a).(\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \widehat{G}_N(s,a).(LN​v)(s)=a∈As​max​GN​(s,a).
(6)

Nothing about approximation or projection has entered yet. For a fixed vvv, Monte Carlo provides unbiased, noisy evaluations of (Lv)(s)(\Bellman v)(s)(Lv)(s) at any state, from draws alone. The maximum over the noisy estimates, however, is not unbiased, and the last section of the chapter is about that.

Sampling the States¶

The second expectation, over the states, is estimated the same way. Galerkin and least-squares conditions have the form ∫R(s;θ) pi(s) ξ(ds)=0\int R(s;\theta)\, p_i(s)\, \xi(ds) = 0∫R(s;θ)pi​(s)ξ(ds)=0 for a distribution ξ\xiξ over states, and the weighted norm of the residual is ∫R(s;θ)2 ξ(ds)\int R(s;\theta)^2\,\xi(ds)∫R(s;θ)2ξ(ds). The weight www of the previous chapters could be any positive function; for sampling it must be a probability distribution that can be drawn from, which is ξ\xiξ after normalization, or any other distribution with importance weights w/ξw/\xiw/ξ. If states S(1),…,S(M)S^{(1)}, \ldots, S^{(M)}S(1),…,S(M) are drawn from ξ\xiξ, each condition becomes a sample average,

∫R(s;θ) pi(s) ξ(ds)≈1M∑m=1MR(S(m);θ) pi(S(m)),\int R(s;\theta)\, p_i(s)\, \xi(ds) \approx \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M R\big(S^{(m)};\theta\big)\, p_i\big(S^{(m)}\big),∫R(s;θ)pi​(s)ξ(ds)≈M1​m=1∑M​R(S(m);θ)pi​(S(m)),
(7)

and the least-squares objective becomes the empirical risk 1M∑mR(S(m);θ)2\frac{1}{M}\sum_m R(S^{(m)};\theta)^2M1​∑m​R(S(m);θ)2. This is the regression of the previous chapter: targets at sampled states, and a fit that minimizes the average error over them. In reinforcement learning ξ\xiξ is rarely chosen; it is the distribution of the states that the data happen to contain, which the previous chapter showed to matter for convergence and the next chapter shows to matter for coverage.

With both expectations sampled, the fitted update is

vk+1=PM L^N vk,v_{k+1} = \Proj_M\, \widehat{\Bellman}_N\, v_k,vk+1​=PM​LN​vk​,
(8)

a fit at MMM sampled states of targets that each average NNN sampled successors. It needs no transition density and no state distribution in closed form, only the ability to draw from them. In the typical reinforcement-learning setting N=1N = 1N=1: each recorded transition (si,ai,ri,si′)(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)(si​,ai​,ri​,si′​) supplies one successor, and the target ri+γv(si′)r_i + \gamma v(s'_i)ri​+γv(si′​) has the full variance of a single draw. The variance is then reduced by the fit, which pools information across neighboring states, and by the number of transitions rather than by averaging at a fixed (s,a)(s,a)(s,a). The section after next returns to this choice.

Action Values¶

The greedy policy of a value function vvv is

π(s)=arg⁡max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a)},\pi(s) = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \Big\{ r(s,a) + \gamma \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a) \Big\},π(s)=arga∈As​max​{r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a)},
(9)

one transition expectation per action at every decision. With a model and a quadrature rule this is a computation; with a simulator it is a Monte Carlo estimate per action, repeated each time the state is visited; with a log it is impossible, because no new successors can be drawn at decision time. The expectation can instead be computed once, during training, and stored. The action-value function of vvv,

q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a),q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a),q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a),
(10)

caches the backup of every action, and the greedy policy becomes π(s)=arg⁡max⁡aq(s,a)\pi(s) = \arg\max_{a} q(s,a)π(s)=argmaxa​q(s,a), a maximization over stored values with no integral and no model. The optimal action-value function q⋆q^\starq⋆ satisfies its own Bellman equation, obtained by substituting v⋆(s′)=max⁡a′q⋆(s′,a′)v^\star(s') = \max_{a'} q^\star(s',a')v⋆(s′)=maxa′​q⋆(s′,a′):

q⋆(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫p(ds′∣s,a) max⁡a′∈As′q⋆(s′,a′).q^\star(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \int p(ds'|s,a)\, \max_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_{s'}} q^\star(s',a').q⋆(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫p(ds′∣s,a)a′∈As′​max​q⋆(s′,a′).
(11)

The right-hand side defines the Bellman operator on action-value functions, (Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ E[max⁡a′q(s′,a′)∣s,a](\Bellman q)(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\max_{a'} q(s',a') \mid s,a](Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γE[maxa′​q(s′,a′)∣s,a], and it is a γ\gammaγ-contraction in the sup norm by the same argument as for vvv: the maximum over a′a'a′ does not increase sup-norm distances, and the expectation does not either. Everything in the previous chapter transfers. Fitted value iteration on qqq is fitted Q-iteration, its error bounds hold with (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) in place of sss, averagers remain safe, and the function class now takes the action as an input or has one output per action. What changes is the cost accounting: the expectations are evaluated during the iterations, at the state-action pairs where targets are computed, and acting afterwards is cheap.

Algorithm 1 (Fitted Q-Iteration with a Model)

The expectation in the target can be computed by quadrature when the model allows it, or estimated by NNN draws of the successor from p(⋅∣s,a)p(\cdot|s,a)p(⋅∣s,a), averaging max⁡a′q(si′,a′)\max_{a'} q(s'_i, a')maxa′​q(si′​,a′) over them. The fitting step is the one of the previous chapter, with its initialization θinit\boldsymbol\theta_{\text{init}}θinit​ and its optimization budget KKK written out because the next chapter varies both.

The Single-Sample Paradigm¶

Most reinforcement learning algorithms do not draw NNN successors per state-action pair. They work with a data set of transition tuples D={(si,ai,ri,si′)}i=1M\mathcal{D} = \{(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)\}_{i=1}^MD={(si​,ai​,ri​,si′​)}i=1M​, each recording the one successor that was observed when aia_iai​ was executed in sis_isi​, and the target of a tuple is yi=ri+γmax⁡a′q(si′,a′)y_i = r_i + \gamma \max_{a'} q(s'_i, a')yi​=ri​+γmaxa′​q(si′​,a′), with N=1N = 1N=1.

This design has two origins. In some settings it is a constraint. A robot that executes an action observes one outcome and cannot rewind to the same state to sample another; the same holds for a clinical trial, a manufacturing process, or any interaction that costs something. Many settings in which reinforcement learning is applied have no such constraint. Game emulators save and restore states, physics simulators reset to any configuration, and software environments are cloned for free. The second origin is historical. Reinforcement learning grew out of models of animal learning, in which an organism experiences one consequence per action and learns from a stream of experience, and temporal-difference learning, Q-learning and the actor-critic methods were designed for that stream.

The convention persisted where the constraint did not, and it shaped the algorithms. They store and manipulate tuples rather than state-action pairs with several successors. They reduce variance through the function approximator, which pools targets from nearby states, and through the number of transitions, rather than by averaging at a fixed (s,a)(s,a)(s,a). And they treat the two expectations asymmetrically: the outer one, over states, is sampled with whatever budget is convenient, a whole data set, a replay buffer of a million transitions, or one transition per step, while the inner one is sampled once. In a domain with a cheap, resettable simulator and high-variance targets, averaging several successors per (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) is a direct variance reduction that current practice rarely uses.

Maximization Bias¶

Each estimate G^N(s,a)\widehat{G}_N(s,a)GN​(s,a) is unbiased, and the maximum over them is not. Fix a state sss and a value function vvv, and write the true continuation value and its estimate as

μ(s,a)=∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a),μ^N(s,a)=1N∑i=1Nv(si′),si′∼p(⋅∣s,a),\mu(s,a) = \int v(s')\,p(ds' \mid s,a), \qquad \hat{\mu}_N(s,a) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N v(s'_i), \quad s'_i \sim p(\cdot|s,a),μ(s,a)=∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a),μ^​N​(s,a)=N1​i=1∑N​v(si′​),si′​∼p(⋅∣s,a),
(12)

so that (L^Nv)(s)=max⁡a{r(s,a)+γμ^N(s,a)}(\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s) = \max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a)\}(LN​v)(s)=maxa​{r(s,a)+γμ^​N​(s,a)}. Let a⋆a^\stara⋆ be the action that maximizes the true backup. The maximum of a collection is at least as large as any of its members, so

E[max⁡a{r(s,a)+γμ^N(s,a)}]≥E[r(s,a⋆)+γμ^N(s,a⋆)]=r(s,a⋆)+γμ(s,a⋆)=(Lv)(s).\mathbb{E}\big[\max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a)\}\big] \ge \mathbb{E}\big[r(s,a^\star) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a^\star)\big] = r(s,a^\star) + \gamma \mu(s,a^\star) = (\Bellman v)(s).E[amax​{r(s,a)+γμ^​N​(s,a)}]≥E[r(s,a⋆)+γμ^​N​(s,a⋆)]=r(s,a⋆)+γμ(s,a⋆)=(Lv)(s).
(13)

The inequality is strict whenever more than one action has a nonzero variance: the maximization picks whichever action received a positive noise, and that inflated estimate becomes the target. This is Jensen’s inequality for the maximum, E[max⁡aYa]≥max⁡aE[Ya]\mathbb{E}[\max_a Y_a] \ge \max_a \mathbb{E}[Y_a]E[maxa​Ya​]≥maxa​E[Ya​], since the maximum is convex. The same inequality is the reason that deterministic policies are optimal in MDPs (Theorem 2), where it says that randomizing over actions cannot beat the best one; here it says that maximizing over noisy estimates cannot be unbiased.

The bias does not average out with more draws of the same estimate, and it compounds. Monte Carlo value iteration vk+1=L^Nvkv_{k+1} = \widehat{\Bellman}_N v_kvk+1​=LN​vk​ builds its targets at iteration k+1k+1k+1 from a vkv_kvk​ that is already biased upward, so E[vk]≥E[vk−1]≥⋯≥v⋆\mathbb{E}[v_k] \ge \mathbb{E}[v_{k-1}] \ge \cdots \ge v^\starE[vk​]≥E[vk−1​]≥⋯≥v⋆, and the inflated values feed back into the next maximization. The cell below holds every true action value at zero, draws five noisy samples per action, and measures the bias of the maximum as the number of actions grows, next to the estimator of the next subsection.

Decoupling Selection from Evaluation¶

The bias comes from using one noisy estimate for two jobs. Decompose the estimate into its mean and its noise, μ^N(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa\hat{\mu}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) + \varepsilon_aμ^​N​(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa​ with E[εa]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_a] = 0E[εa​]=0. The standard target is

Y=r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)+γεa^,a^=arg⁡max⁡a{r(s,a)+γμ(s,a)+γεa},Y = r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a) + \gamma \varepsilon_{\hat a}, \qquad \hat a = \arg\max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \mu(s,a) + \gamma \varepsilon_a\},Y=r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)+γεa^​,a^=argamax​{r(s,a)+γμ(s,a)+γεa​},
(14)

and the same εa^\varepsilon_{\hat a}εa^​ that made a^\hat aa^ win is added to its value. Double Q-learning Van Hasselt et al. (2016) breaks this coupling with two independent estimates of every action, μ^N(1)(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa(1)\hat{\mu}^{(1)}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) + \varepsilon^{(1)}_aμ^​N(1)​(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa(1)​ and μ^N(2)(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa(2)\hat{\mu}^{(2)}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) + \varepsilon^{(2)}_aμ^​N(2)​(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa(2)​, with ε(1)\varepsilon^{(1)}ε(1) and ε(2)\varepsilon^{(2)}ε(2) independent. The first selects and the second evaluates:

a^=arg⁡max⁡a{r(s,a)+γμ^N(1)(s,a)},Y=r(s,a^)+γμ^N(2)(s,a^).\hat a = \arg\max_{a} \big\{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}^{(1)}_N(s,a)\big\}, \qquad Y = r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}^{(2)}_N(s,\hat a).a^=argamax​{r(s,a)+γμ^​N(1)​(s,a)},Y=r(s,a^)+γμ^​N(2)​(s,a^).
(15)

The selected action a^\hat aa^ is random, a function of ε(1)\varepsilon^{(1)}ε(1) alone. Conditioning on it,

E[Y]=Eε(1)[Eε(2)[r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)+γεa^(2)∣a^]]=Eε(1)[r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)],\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(1)}}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(2)}}\big[r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a) + \gamma \varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a} \mid \hat a\big]\Big] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(1)}}\big[r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a)\big],E[Y]=Eε(1)​[Eε(2)​[r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)+γεa^(2)​∣a^]]=Eε(1)​[r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)],
(16)

because ε(2)\varepsilon^{(2)}ε(2) is independent of a^\hat aa^, so that E[εa^(2)∣a^]=E[εa^(2)]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a} \mid \hat a] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a}] = 0E[εa^(2)​∣a^]=E[εa^(2)​]=0. The evaluation noise contributes nothing on average. What remains is the selection bias: a^\hat aa^ is more often an action whose ε(1)\varepsilon^{(1)}ε(1) was positive than one whose true value is highest, so E[μ(s,a^)]≤max⁡aμ(s,a)\mathbb{E}[\mu(s,\hat a)] \le \max_a \mu(s,a)E[μ(s,a^)]≤maxa​μ(s,a), and the double estimator is biased downward. In Figure 2 the maximum estimator grows more optimistic as the number of actions grows, while the double estimator has no bias: every action has the same true value there, so selecting the wrong one costs nothing and the selection bias is zero. When the true values differ, the double estimator is biased downward instead, by much less than the maximum is biased upward. Removing the evaluation bias, the reuse of the winning noise, removes most of the overestimation.

Remark 1 (Two Q-functions instead of two sets of draws)

The argument assumes two independent sets of draws from p(⋅∣s,a)p(\cdot|s,a)p(⋅∣s,a) for every state-action pair, which a log never provides and a simulator provides only by resetting. The practical implementation keeps two Q-functions instead, trained on different data or updated at different times, for instance an online network and a slowly updated copy of it. Their errors are then less correlated than the errors of a single network used twice, which gives part of the independence that the argument needs. This is Double DQN, in the next chapter (Double DQN).

The algorithm below writes the principle out with Monte Carlo targets. Two Q-functions alternate roles: at line 9 the first selects the action and at line 12 the second evaluates it, and lines 10 and 13 do the same with the roles exchanged. The mechanism is the same whether the Q-functions are tables or fitted functions, and with single-sample data (N=1N = 1N=1) the two Q-functions are trained on different subsets or at different frequencies to approximate the independence.

Algorithm 2 (Double Q Value Iteration with Monte Carlo)

Input: MDP, state sample S\mathcal{S}S, Monte Carlo sample size NNN, maximum iterations KKK

  2. k←0k \leftarrow 0k←0

  3. repeat

  4. \quad for each s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S do

  5. \quad\quad for each a∈A(s)a \in \mathcal{A}(s)a∈A(s) do

  6. \quad\quad\quad Draw NNN next states: s1′,…,sN′∼p(⋅∣s,a)s'_1, \ldots, s'_N \sim p(\cdot \mid s,a)s1′​,…,sN′​∼p(⋅∣s,a)

  8. \quad\quad\quad for i=1,…,Ni = 1, \ldots, Ni=1,…,N do

  9. \quad\quad\quad\quad ai(1)←arg⁡max⁡a′qk(1)(si′,a′)a^{(1)}_i \leftarrow \arg\max_{a'} q^{(1)}_k(s'_i, a')ai(1)​←argmaxa′​qk(1)​(si′​,a′)

  10. \quad\quad\quad\quad ai(2)←arg⁡max⁡a′qk(2)(si′,a′)a^{(2)}_i \leftarrow \arg\max_{a'} q^{(2)}_k(s'_i, a')ai(2)​←argmaxa′​qk(2)​(si′​,a′)

Other Corrections¶

Three other approaches keep a single estimate and correct the maximum itself. They differ in how much they assume about the noise.

The correction can be learned. Keane & Wolpin (1994) treated the bias δ(s)=E[(L^Nv)(s)]−(Lv)(s)≥0\delta(s) = \mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s)] - (\Bellman v)(s) \ge 0δ(s)=E[(LN​v)(s)]−(Lv)(s)≥0 as a quantity to estimate and subtract. It cannot be computed directly, but it depends on observable features of the state: the number of actions, the sample size, and the spread of the action values, since the bias is large when several actions are close and small when one dominates. At a small set of states, they ran both a high-fidelity evaluation of the backup, with many draws, and the NNN-draw estimate used by the iteration, and regressed the gap on those features; during value iteration the predicted bias is subtracted from the raw maximum. The template, simulate on a subset and interpolate everywhere, is common in econometric dynamic programming. It has seen little use in reinforcement learning, because the high-fidelity evaluations are expensive and a misspecified regression feeds its own error back into the values.

The correction can be derived, under a distributional assumption. Lee et al. (2013)Lee & Powell (2019) assumed Gaussian noise of standard deviation σ\sigmaσ on the estimates of MMM actions, in which case the expected maximum of the noises follows from extreme value theory,

E[max⁡aεa]≈σ(CEbM+bM),bM=2log⁡M−log⁡log⁡M−log⁡4π,\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_{a} \varepsilon_a\Big] \approx \sigma \left(\frac{C_{\mathrm{E}}}{b_M} + b_M\right), \qquad b_M = \sqrt{2\log M - \log\log M - \log 4\pi},E[amax​εa​]≈σ(bM​CE​​+bM​),bM​=2logM−loglogM−log4π​,
(17)

with CE≈0.5772C_{\mathrm{E}} \approx 0.5772CE​≈0.5772 the Euler–Mascheroni constant, and the target is corrected by subtracting this amount with σ\sigmaσ estimated from repeated rewards at the same (s,a)(s,a)(s,a). The formula is exact for a single-state problem whose only noise is in the rewards, and it is a first-order correction otherwise; with heavier tails than Gaussian it undercorrects. It replaces the regression of the learned correction by a closed form, at the price of the Gaussian assumption.

The maximum can be replaced. D'Eramo et al. (2016) weight each action by the probability that it is the best one under a Gaussian model of the estimates, wa=P(a∈arg⁡max⁡a′μ^a′)w_a = \mathbb{P}\big(a \in \arg\max_{a'} \hat{\mu}_{a'}\big)wa​=P(a∈argmaxa′​μ^​a′​), and use ∑awaμ^a\sum_a w_a \hat{\mu}_a∑a​wa​μ^​a​ in place of max⁡aμ^a\max_a \hat{\mu}_amaxa​μ^​a​. The weighted estimator sits between the optimism of the maximum and the pessimism of the double estimator, and adapts to the gaps between actions: when one action dominates its weight is near one and the estimator is the maximum, and when several are close their estimates are averaged. It needs a variance estimate per action and one integral per action, which limits it to small action sets. The smooth Bellman operator of the regularized chapter also replaces the hard maximum by an average, with weights set by a temperature rather than by estimated uncertainty. A last option changes neither the target nor the operator but the loss of the fit, so that overestimates are penalized more than underestimates; the next chapter takes it up with Gumbel regression.

Exercises¶

The exercises move from single estimators to their effect inside the iteration. The first ones are short checks; Exercise 6 is a short simulation.

Exercise 1 (Sign before simulation)

Several actions have equal true values and independent noisy estimates. What sign do you expect for the bias of their maximum?

Solution to Exercise 1

Positive. Maximization preferentially selects estimates with favorable noise, so the expected maximum exceeds the common true value.

Exercise 2 (Double estimation)

Which dependence is broken when one estimate selects the maximizing action and an independent estimate evaluates it, and which bias remains?

Solution to Exercise 2

The evaluation noise is made independent of the lucky noise that caused the selection, which removes the reuse of the same positive error for both jobs. The selection bias remains: the chosen action is still more often one whose first estimate was lucky, so the double estimator is biased slightly downward.

Exercise 3 (Sample sizes)

A simulator returns successor values with standard deviation σ=3\sigma = 3σ=3.

  1. How many draws give a root mean squared error of 0.01 for one expectation?

  2. A fitted iteration needs one such expectation for each of 2,000 states and 4 actions. How many simulator calls does one iteration cost, and how would the cost change if the state had twice as many coordinates?

  3. By Theorem 1, what does an integration error of 0.01 per iteration contribute to the final value error with γ=0.95\gamma = 0.95γ=0.95?

Solution to Exercise 3

  1. σ/N=0.01\sigma/\sqrt N = 0.01σ/N​=0.01 gives N=(3/0.01)2=90,000N = (3/0.01)^2 = 90{,}000N=(3/0.01)2=90,000.

  2. 2,000×4×90,000=7.2×1082{,}000 \times 4 \times 90{,}000 = 7.2 \times 10^82,000×4×90,000=7.2×108 calls per iteration. The Monte Carlo rate does not depend on the dimension, so the count does not change unless σ\sigmaσ does; a product quadrature rule would need NDN^DND nodes instead.

  3. At most 0.01/(1−0.95)=0.20.01/(1 - 0.95) = 0.20.01/(1−0.95)=0.2, added to the error of the fit.

Exercise 4 (The bias of a maximum)

Two actions have the same true value 0, and each is estimated by the mean of five draws of standard deviation 1.

  1. Show that the expected maximum of the two estimates is σmean/π\sigma_{\text{mean}}/\sqrt\piσmean​/π​, where σmean=1/5\sigma_{\text{mean}} = 1/\sqrt5σmean​=1/5​ is the standard deviation of each mean, and evaluate it. Hint: the maximum of two numbers is their average plus half their absolute difference.

  2. Compare with the first point of Figure 2.

  3. How does the bias change with NNN, the number of draws per action?

Solution to Exercise 4

  1. max⁡(X1,X2)=12(X1+X2)+12∣X1−X2∣\max(X_1, X_2) = \tfrac12(X_1 + X_2) + \tfrac12|X_1 - X_2|max(X1​,X2​)=21​(X1​+X2​)+21​∣X1​−X2​∣. The first term has mean 0. The difference is Gaussian with standard deviation 2 σmean\sqrt2\,\sigma_{\text{mean}}2​σmean​, and E∣Z∣=2/π\mathbb{E}|Z| = \sqrt{2/\pi}E∣Z∣=2/π​ for a standard Gaussian, so the expectation is 122 σmean2/π=σmean/π=1/5π≈0.252\tfrac12\sqrt2\,\sigma_{\text{mean}}\sqrt{2/\pi} = \sigma_{\text{mean}}/\sqrt\pi = 1/\sqrt{5\pi} \approx 0.25221​2​σmean​2/π​=σmean​/π​=1/5π​≈0.252.

  2. The figure shows 0.25 at two actions.

  3. It scales with σmean=1/N\sigma_{\text{mean}} = 1/\sqrt Nσmean​=1/N​: four times as many draws halve it. It never vanishes for finite NNN.

Exercise 5 (When the double estimator does worse)

Two actions have true values μ1=0\mu_1 = 0μ1​=0 and μ2=−1\mu_2 = -1μ2​=−1, and each estimate has Gaussian noise of standard deviation 1.

  1. For the maximum estimator, use E[max⁡(X1,X2)]=μ1Φ(δ/ϑ)+μ2Φ(−δ/ϑ)+ϑ ϕ(δ/ϑ)\mathbb{E}[\max(X_1, X_2)] = \mu_1\Phi(\delta/\vartheta) + \mu_2\Phi(-\delta/\vartheta) + \vartheta\,\phi(\delta/\vartheta)E[max(X1​,X2​)]=μ1​Φ(δ/ϑ)+μ2​Φ(−δ/ϑ)+ϑϕ(δ/ϑ) with δ=μ1−μ2\delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2δ=μ1​−μ2​ and ϑ=2\vartheta = \sqrt2ϑ=2​, where Φ\PhiΦ and ϕ\phiϕ are the standard Gaussian distribution and density, to compute its bias.

  2. For the double estimator, the selected action is wrong with probability Φ(−δ/ϑ)\Phi(-\delta/\vartheta)Φ(−δ/ϑ). Compute its bias.

  3. Which estimator is closer to the truth here? Relate the answer to the two sources of bias in Maximization Bias, and to the case of equal values in Figure 2.

Solution to Exercise 5

  1. Φ(−1/2)=0.240\Phi(-1/\sqrt2) = 0.240Φ(−1/2​)=0.240 and ϕ(1/2)=0.311\phi(1/\sqrt2) = 0.311ϕ(1/2​)=0.311, so the expected maximum is −0.240+2×0.311=0.200-0.240 + \sqrt2 \times 0.311 = 0.200−0.240+2​×0.311=0.200, a bias of +0.20.

  2. The double estimator is unbiased for the value of the action it selects, so its expectation is −1×0.240=−0.240-1 \times 0.240 = -0.240−1×0.240=−0.240, a bias of -0.24. A simulation with 2×1062 \times 10^62×106 draws gives 0.200 and -0.238.

  3. The maximum estimator is closer here, by a little. With equal values the selection costs nothing and the double estimator is unbiased; with a gap of the size of the noise, selection bias dominates, and it is negative. Removing evaluation bias does not remove selection bias, which is why the double estimator is pessimistic rather than unbiased in general.

Exercise 6 (Bias that compounds)

Consider one state and MMM actions, each with reward 0 observed through Gaussian noise of standard deviation 1, and γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9. Monte Carlo value iteration sets vk+1=max⁡ar^a+γvkv_{k+1} = \max_a \hat r_a + \gamma v_kvk+1​=maxa​r^a​+γvk​, where each r^a\hat r_ar^a​ is a fresh mean of NNN draws.

  2. Simulate it for M=4M = 4M=4 and N=5N = 5N=5, and compare with b≈0.46b \approx 0.46b≈0.46 read from Figure 2.

  3. Replace the maximum by the double estimator, with two independent sets of draws, and simulate again.

  2. With b≈0.460b \approx 0.460b≈0.460 the limit is 4.6, ten times the per-step bias. A simulation such as

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
M, N, gamma, runs, iterations = 4, 5, 0.9, 20000, 200
v = np.zeros(runs)
for _ in range(iterations):

  1. Show that (Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ E[max⁡a′q(s′,a′)∣s,a](\Bellman q)(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\max_{a'} q(s',a') \mid s,a](Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γE[maxa′​q(s′,a′)∣s,a] is a γ\gammaγ-contraction in the sup norm. Solution to Exercise 7

  1. For each (s,a)(s,a)(s,a), ∣(Lq)(s,a)−(Lq′)(s,a)∣≤γ E[∣max⁡a′q(s′,a′)−max⁡a′q′(s′,a′)∣]≤γ∥q−q′∥∞|(\Bellman q)(s,a) - (\Bellman q')(s,a)| \le \gamma\,\mathbb{E}\big[|\max_{a'} q(s',a') - \max_{a'} q'(s',a')|\big] \le \gamma\|q - q'\|_\infty∣(Lq)(s,a)−(Lq′)(s,a)∣≤γE[∣maxa′​q(s′,a′)−maxa′​q′(s′,a′)∣]≤γ∥q−q′∥∞​.

  2. π⋆(s)∈arg⁡max⁡aq⋆(s,a)\pi^\star(s) \in \arg\max_a q^\star(s,a)π⋆(s)∈argmaxa​q⋆(s,a) and v⋆(s)=max⁡aq⋆(s,a)v^\star(s) = \max_a q^\star(s,a)v⋆(s)=maxa​q⋆(s,a). Neither needs the model, which is the point of storing qqq.

  3. Fitted Q-iteration computes targets for every state-action pair, ∣A∣|\mathcal{A}|∣A∣ times as many as fitted value iteration with a model, but acting with it is a maximization over stored values, with no expectation to estimate.

Exercise 8 (Many successors or many transitions)

A resettable simulator can return several successors of the same state and action. With a fixed budget of simulator calls per iteration, compare two uses on the eight-dimensional stopping problem of the previous chapter: many states with one successor each, or a quarter as many states with four successors each. Measure the error of the fitted value function and of its greedy policy, and explain the result with the two expectations of Two Expectations in Every Fitted Update: which error does each choice reduce?

Solution to Exercise 8

This exercise is open-ended. More successors per state reduce the variance of each target, which a regression would otherwise have to average out across nearby states. More states reduce the error of the fit itself and extend coverage. Which wins depends on the noise of the targets relative to the smoothness of the value: a problem with very noisy transitions and a smooth value favors more successors, and a problem whose value varies a lot across the state space favors more states.

Summary and Forward Look¶

Fitted Bellman updates contain two expectations, inside the operator and over the states, and either can be estimated from samples. The sample average is unbiased, its error falls as N−1/2N^{-1/2}N−1/2 whatever the dimension, and it adds a per-iteration error that the bound of the previous chapter absorbs. Sampling makes the model optional: a simulator or a log of transitions suffices, which is the setting of reinforcement learning. Acting on a sampled value function would require sampling at decision time, so the action-value function q(s,a)q(s,a)q(s,a) stores the backup of each action instead, and fitted Q-iteration is fitted value iteration on qqq. The maximum over noisy estimates is biased upward, and the bias compounds through the iterations; using one estimate to select the action and an independent one to value it removes the larger part of the bias, and learned, analytic or weighted corrections are the alternatives.

The algorithms of this chapter still choose the states at which targets are computed, and still draw as many successors as they like. Learning from logged and online data take the data as given: a fixed log of transitions with one successor each, or a buffer that fills as the agent acts, and a fit that is warm-started and stopped early. The remaining design choices of the practical algorithms are choices about that data and that fit.
